beats.caption: Text is cut into tokens, and each token becomes a vector
beats.text: A large language model (LLM) never sees letters. Text is split into tokens (whole words or word pieces, about 3/4 of a word each on average) and every token is looked up in a table that turns it into a long list of numbers, its embedding, a few thousand numbers wide.

beats.caption: Dozens of transformer layers; attention links each token to earlier ones
beats.text: The vectors pass up through a stack of transformer layers, often 30 to 120 of them. In each, attention lets every token pull in information from the tokens before it (which word 'it' refers to, say), then a feed-forward block transforms each one. The layers' weights are the parameters.

beats.caption: The top scores every possible next token; one is picked and appended
beats.text: At the top, the model outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary (often 100,000+). One is chosen, added to the end of the text, and the whole stack runs again for the next. That one-token-at-a-time loop is all a chat answer is.

beats.caption: Billions to trillions of parameters, sliced across many GPUs
beats.text: Models range from a few billion parameters to over a trillion. At 2 bytes each, a 400B model is ~800 GB, far more than one GPU's HBM, so the weights are split across 8 or more GPUs linked by fast interconnect, which pass activations between them every layer.

beats.caption: Trained on trillions of tokens, served to millions of users
beats.text: Learning those weights takes months of training on tens of thousands of GPUs; serving them takes large inference fleets. LLMs underpin chat assistants, coding tools and enterprise AI, and drive demand for GPUs, HBM and networking: Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOGL), Meta (META), NVIDIA (NVDA).
